list.listitem: Malignant hyperthermia is a rare inherited disorder leading to a syndrome of hypermetabolism after exposure to volatile anesthetics agents or depolarizing muscle relaxants such as succinylcholine. C
Typical symptoms include muscular rigidity, evidence of muscle breakdown, respiratory acidosis, temperature elevation, cardiac changes, and family history of malignant hyperthermia. B
Treatment is by cessation of anesthesia, administration of dantrolene, active cooling, and hyperventilation. B
Malignant hyperthermia is usually fatal if not identified early. B

background.definition: Susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia is an inherited disorder in which anesthetic agents trigger skeletal muscle hypermetabolism resulting in elevated body temperature. It was first characterized in 1962.

list.listitem: Approximately 1:15,000 in children and 1:50,000 in adults undergoing general anesthetic procedures.
Caused by mutations in the ryanodine receptor gene.
It is an autosomal dominant condition for most familial patterns of inheritance, with variable penetrance and expressivity.
It may occur after subsequent exposure to triggering anesthetic.
There are at least four chromosomal locations (3, 7, 17, 19q13).
Mutations affect the ryanodine receptor RYR1, a calcium release channel of skeletal muscle.
Actin-myosin coupling leads to muscle rigidity and high free calcium in the myoplasm, which leads in turn to uncontrolled muscle activity, acidosis, and heat production.
Malignant hyperthermia can only be prevented by thorough interview and history of previous anesthetic experience of the patient and family. C
Risk stratification is possible using the Larach Protocol guidelines (). B

Diagnosis is based on clinical findings related to volatile anesthetic use and the hypermetabolic findings including muscular rigidity, evidence of muscle breakdown, respiratory acidosis, temperature elevation, cardiac changes, and family history of malignant hyperthermia. B
Formal diagnostic criteria are shown in . C

Differential.Differential_Features: Due to allergic reaction, fever, inadequate general anesthesia, hypovolemia, and pheochromocytoma
Due to rebreathing, increased dead space, hypermetabolic state, fever
Due to drug reaction, septicemia, iatrogenic overwarming, measurement error

list.listitem: The past medical history may contain known or suspected episodes of malignant hyperthermia in the patient or in a family member. However, a retrospective study of more than 6,200 patients who were genetically screened for inherited diseases showed significant discordance between family history and results of genetic testing. Specifically, among the 90 patients who had a positive genetic screen for inherited conditions, 66% had a negative family history. The discordance appears highest for malignant hyperthermia, cardiomyopathy, and arrhythmia. Hence the authors recommend considering genetic testing for these conditions if family history is unrevealing.

Patients typically present with a variety of cardiac, respiratory, and muscular system findings including rapid temperature rise, tachycardia, tachypnea, masseter muscle rigidity, and generalized muscle rigidity.
They may also have arrhythmias, cyanosis, skin mottling, diaphoresis, evidence of coagulopathy, and hemodynamic instability.
Typical laboratory findings include hypercarbia, hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria, rhabdomyolysis, and respiratory and/or metabolic acidosis.

The halothane caffeine contracture test is a muscle biopsy test whereby a viable muscle biopsy specimen is connected to a force transducer and exposed to halothane or caffeine. Induced muscle contracture is considered diagnostic of malignant hyperthermia. The test is 97% sensitive and 78% specific (LR+ 4.4, LR− 0.04).
Consider confirmatory testing if the patient has a suspected or known history of malignant hyperthermia or if there is a family history of malignant hyperthermia.
The 1994 Consensus Conference for Diagnosis and Prediction of Malignant Hyperthermia established a set of diagnostic criteria based on six processes and other factors.
Each indication is assigned a point value; the higher the score, the more likely the diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia (see ).
Diagnosis is primarily clinical in a patient with muscular rigidity, muscle breakdown, respiratory acidosis, temperature increase, and cardiac involvement following general anesthesia.
Confirm the diagnosis with application of the Larach guidelines or contracture testing.
Confirmatory testing may be indicated due to prior suspected or known history of malignant hyperthermia or a family history of malignant hyperthermia.
Cessation of general anesthetic is the initial treatment step; acetaminophen and cooling blanket may also help. C
Dantrolene is the only medical treatment. Dose is IV bolus 2.5 mg/kg repeated every 5 minutes until symptoms resolve, followed by continuous infusion of dantrolene 10 mg/kg/d for 24 hours. B
Give acetaminophen and immediately cease administration of general anesthetic.

Dantrolene is the only medical treatment; it directly inhibits the excitation-contraction mechanisms in skeletal muscle. It is thought to inhibit the ryanodine receptor, blocking the uncontrolled release of intracellular calcium stores from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Usual dose is dantrolene IV bolus 2.5 mg/kg (through large bore IV) repeated every 5 minutes until symptoms resolve, followed by continuous infusion of dantrolene 10 mg/kg/d for 24 hours.
Side effects associated with IV dantrolene use include: muscle weakness (22%), phlebitis at the infusion site (10%), respiratory failure (3%), and GI discomfort (3%).

Extravascular infusion of dantrolene can cause severe tissue necrosis; therefore, dantrolene should be given via central venous catheter. Other complications include drowsiness, confusion, dizziness, and diarrhea after oral administration.

Active cooling is recommended for temperature greater than 39°C and can be discontinued when the patient's temperature reaches 38°C. Use refrigerated IV crystalloid boluses, apply ice packs to groin and axilla, or use a cooling blanket.
When patient has severe metabolic acidosis requiring IV sodium bicarbonate, temporary hyperventilation may be required to offset the additional CO2 generated.
Mortality prior to dantrolene therapy approached 70% to 80%. Current mortality is less than 10% with early identification, rapid therapy, and IV dantrolene. B

feature.caption: The 1994 Consensus Clinical Grading Scale (Larach Guidelines) for Malignant Hyperthermia.
feature.feature_body:
Symptom Point Range
Process I (rigidity):generalized muscular rigidity or masseter spasm after succinylcholine 0-30
Process II (muscle breakdown): elevated CK with or without succinylcholine, cola-colored urine, myoglobin in urine or serum, serum potassium greater than 6 mEq/L 0-53
Process III (respiratory acidosis): increased end-tidal or arterial CO2 levels with appropriate or spontaneous ventilation, hypercarbia or tacypnea 0-85
Process IV (temperature increase): inappropriately rapid increase in temperature or inappropriately increased temperature 0-25
Process V (cardiac involvement): inappropriate sinus tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation 0-6
Process VI (family history): positive family history of malignant hyperthermia in a first-degree relative 0-20
Other factors: arterial pH <7.25, arterial base excesses more negative than −8 mEq/L, rapid reversal of malignant hyperthermia after IV dantrolene administration 0-45
Total points:
Interpretation Score
Almost never 0
Unlikely 3-9
Somewhat less than likely 10-19
Somewhat greater than likely 20-34
Very likely 35-49
Almost certain 50+
From Larach MG, Localio AR, Allen GC, et al. A clinical grading scale to predict malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. Anesthesiology 1994:80;771–779.
